meta.subject: english
meta.description: Literature facts: literary devices, genres, famous works, literary movements, figurative language, point of view, characterization, plot elements

facts.statement: A simile compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as': 'Her smile was like sunshine'
A metaphor compares two unlike things without using 'like' or 'as': 'Time is money'
Personification gives human qualities to nonhuman things: 'The wind whispered through the trees'
Alliteration is the repetition of the same beginning consonant sound in nearby words: 'Peter Piper picked a peck'
Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration for emphasis: 'I've told you a million times'
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates the sound it represents: buzz, hiss, splash, pop, bang
Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens; it has three main types: verbal, situational, and dramatic
Foreshadowing provides hints or clues about events that will happen later in the story
Symbolism uses an object, person, or event to represent a deeper meaning or idea beyond its literal sense
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell) to create vivid mental pictures
An oxymoron combines two contradictory words: 'jumbo shrimp,' 'bittersweet,' 'deafening silence'
A paradox is a statement that seems contradictory but reveals a deeper truth: 'Less is more'
Repetition is deliberately using a word or phrase more than once to create emphasis or rhythm
A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not to get an answer: 'Isn't it a beautiful day?'
Verbal irony is saying the opposite of what you mean, such as calling a stormy day 'lovely weather'

common_errors.wrong: metaphors use 'like' or 'as'
common_errors.correct: Metaphors do NOT use 'like' or 'as.' That is a simile. A metaphor states the comparison directly: 'Life is a journey.'

common_errors.wrong: irony is the same as coincidence
common_errors.correct: Irony involves a contrast between expectation and reality. A fire station burning down is ironic; rain on a random day is just coincidence.

common_errors.wrong: alliteration requires all words to start with the same letter
common_errors.correct: Alliteration requires the same beginning SOUND, not letter. 'Phone photo' has alliteration (same 'f' sound) even though the letters differ.

common_errors.wrong: an oxymoron and a paradox are the same device
common_errors.correct: An oxymoron is a two-word phrase with contradictory terms ('living dead'). A paradox is a full statement that seems contradictory but reveals truth.

facts.statement: Fiction is literature created from the imagination; nonfiction is based on real events and facts
Poetry uses rhythmic and often figurative language, organized into lines and stanzas rather than paragraphs
Drama is literature written to be performed, consisting of dialogue and stage directions
Fantasy involves magical or supernatural elements that do not exist in the real world
Historical fiction is set in a real historical period and blends fictional characters or events with real history
A biography tells the story of a person's life written by someone else; an autobiography is written by the person themselves
A memoir focuses on specific memories or periods of the author's life, unlike an autobiography which covers their whole life
A fable is a short story that teaches a moral lesson and often features talking animals, such as Aesop's fables
A myth is a traditional story that explains natural phenomena or a culture's beliefs, often involving gods and heroes
A legend is a traditional story about a historical figure that may be partly true but has been exaggerated over time, such as King Arthur
Science fiction imagines future technology, space travel, or scientific advances and explores their consequences
Realistic fiction portrays characters and events that could happen in real life but are made up by the author

common_errors.wrong: all stories that seem real are nonfiction
common_errors.correct: Realistic fiction features believable characters and settings but is still made up. Only nonfiction is based on actual facts and events.

common_errors.wrong: biography and autobiography are the same
common_errors.correct: A biography is written by someone else about a person. An autobiography is written by the person about themselves.

common_errors.wrong: poetry must rhyme
common_errors.correct: Many forms of poetry do not rhyme, including free verse, haiku, and blank verse. Rhyme is one tool poets use but not a requirement.

common_errors.wrong: myths and legends are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Myths explain natural phenomena and feature gods or supernatural beings. Legends are based on real historical figures whose stories have been exaggerated.

common_errors.wrong: fables and fairy tales are the same
common_errors.correct: Fables are short stories with a clear moral lesson, often with animal characters. Fairy tales involve magic and fantasy but don't always teach a moral.

facts.statement: Plot is the sequence of events in a story: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution
The climax is the turning point or most intense moment of the story
Setting is the time and place in which a story takes place
Theme is the central message or underlying meaning of a story, not just what happens but what it means
Conflict is the struggle between opposing forces; it can be internal (within a character) or external (with another character, nature, or society)
The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist is the character or force that opposes the protagonist
First-person point of view uses 'I' and shows one character's thoughts; third-person can be limited (one character's perspective) or omniscient (all characters)
The exposition introduces the characters, setting, and basic situation at the beginning of a story
Rising action includes the events that build tension and lead up to the climax
Falling action includes events that happen after the climax as the story moves toward resolution
The resolution (denouement) is the final part of the story where loose ends are tied up and the conflict is resolved

common_errors.wrong: theme and topic are the same thing
common_errors.correct: A topic is what a story is about (e.g., 'friendship'). A theme is the message about that topic (e.g., 'true friends support each other through hard times').

common_errors.wrong: the protagonist is always the hero and the antagonist is always the villain
common_errors.correct: The protagonist is simply the main character, and the antagonist is the opposing force. Neither needs to be morally good or evil.

common_errors.wrong: the climax is the end of the story
common_errors.correct: The climax is the turning point, not the ending. After the climax comes the falling action and resolution.

common_errors.wrong: all stories must have a happy resolution
common_errors.correct: Stories can end in many ways: happy, sad, ambiguous, or open-ended. A resolution simply means the conflict is addressed, not that everything works out.

facts.statement: First-person point of view uses pronouns 'I,' 'me,' and 'my' and tells the story from one character's perspective
Second-person point of view uses the pronoun 'you' and addresses the reader directly, as in choose-your-own-adventure books
Third-person limited tells the story from outside using 'he,' 'she,' or 'they,' but only shows one character's thoughts and feelings
Third-person omniscient tells the story from outside and knows the thoughts and feelings of all characters
An unreliable narrator is a character whose telling of the story cannot be fully trusted because of bias, limited knowledge, or dishonesty
The point of view an author chooses affects how much the reader knows about the characters and events
In first-person narration, the reader can only know what the narrator sees, thinks, and experiences
Third-person objective point of view reports only what can be seen and heard, without revealing any character's thoughts

common_errors.wrong: first person and third person limited give the same information
common_errors.correct: First person is told BY a character using 'I.' Third person limited is told by an outside narrator about one character using 'he/she.' The narrator voice differs.

common_errors.wrong: omniscient means the narrator is a character in the story
common_errors.correct: An omniscient narrator is an all-knowing voice OUTSIDE the story who can see into every character's mind. They are not a character.

common_errors.wrong: second-person point of view is very common in novels
common_errors.correct: Second-person POV is rare in novels. It is more common in choose-your-own-adventure books, instructions, and some experimental fiction.

facts.statement: Direct characterization is when the author explicitly tells the reader about a character's traits: 'She was brave and kind'
Indirect characterization reveals a character through their actions, speech, thoughts, appearance, and what others say about them
A round character is complex with many traits, like a real person; a flat character has only one or two traits
A dynamic character changes and grows throughout the story; a static character remains the same
Character motivation is the reason or driving force behind a character's actions and decisions
Dialogue reveals character personality, relationships, and emotions through what characters say and how they say it
A foil is a character who contrasts with the main character to highlight particular qualities of each
An archetype is a typical character type that recurs across many stories, such as the hero, mentor, trickster, or villain
Character traits are qualities that describe how a character thinks, feels, and behaves, such as honest, shy, or courageous

common_errors.wrong: a dynamic character is the same as an interesting character
common_errors.correct: A dynamic character is one who CHANGES during the story. A character can be interesting and entertaining but still be static (unchanged).

common_errors.wrong: flat characters are always bad writing
common_errors.correct: Flat characters serve a purpose in stories, especially minor characters. Not every character needs to be fully developed.

common_errors.wrong: the antagonist is always a person
common_errors.correct: The antagonist can be a person, a force of nature, society, technology, or even the main character's own inner conflict.

facts.statement: Figurative language uses words in a non-literal way to create vivid images, comparisons, or effects
An idiom is a phrase whose meaning cannot be understood from the individual words: 'It's raining cats and dogs' means raining heavily
A pun is a play on words that uses multiple meanings or similar sounds for humorous effect: 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana'
An analogy compares two different things to explain an idea: 'The heart is like a pump for blood'
An allegory is a story where characters and events represent deeper moral or political meanings, like George Orwell's 'Animal Farm'
An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known person, event, place, or work of art: 'He has the Midas touch'
A euphemism is a mild or gentle word or phrase used in place of something harsh or unpleasant: 'passed away' instead of 'died'
Understatement deliberately makes something seem less important or serious than it is, often for ironic or humorous effect
Tone is the author's attitude toward the subject, revealed through word choice, and can be serious, humorous, sarcastic, or formal
Mood is the emotional feeling a piece of writing creates in the reader, such as suspenseful, joyful, or gloomy

common_errors.wrong: tone and mood are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Tone is the author's attitude (how the writer feels). Mood is the feeling the reader gets. A sarcastic tone might create an uneasy mood.

common_errors.wrong: idioms mean exactly what the words say
common_errors.correct: Idioms have figurative meanings that differ from literal words. 'Break a leg' means 'good luck,' not to literally break a leg.

common_errors.wrong: an allusion and an illusion are the same
common_errors.correct: An allusion is a literary reference to something well-known. An illusion is something that deceives the senses or mind.

common_errors.wrong: all figurative language is the same as metaphor
common_errors.correct: Metaphor is one type of figurative language. The category also includes simile, personification, hyperbole, idiom, allusion, and many others.

facts.statement: Romanticism (late 1700s-mid 1800s) emphasized emotion, imagination, nature, and individualism over reason and order
Realism (mid-late 1800s) portrayed everyday life and ordinary people accurately, without romantic idealization
Modernism (early 1900s) experimented with new forms, stream of consciousness, and reflected the disillusionment after World War I
The Harlem Renaissance (1920s-1930s) was a cultural movement celebrating African American art, music, and literature, featuring writers like Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston
Transcendentalism (1830s-1850s) emphasized self-reliance, intuition, and a spiritual connection with nature, led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau
Gothic literature features dark, mysterious settings, supernatural elements, and themes of fear and death, as in Poe's works
The Renaissance (1300s-1600s) was a cultural rebirth in Europe that revived classical learning and produced writers like Shakespeare and Dante
Naturalism (late 1800s) depicted characters controlled by forces of nature, environment, and heredity, showing life without moral judgment

common_errors.wrong: Romanticism is about romantic love stories
common_errors.correct: Literary Romanticism is about emotion, nature, imagination, and individuality — not specifically about love stories.

common_errors.wrong: the Harlem Renaissance was only about music
common_errors.correct: The Harlem Renaissance included literature, poetry, visual art, theater, and music. Writers like Langston Hughes were central to the movement.

common_errors.wrong: realism and naturalism are identical literary movements
common_errors.correct: Realism depicts everyday life accurately. Naturalism goes further, showing characters as products of heredity and environment, often with a deterministic worldview.

facts.statement: William Shakespeare wrote approximately 37 plays and 154 sonnets in the late 1500s and early 1600s
'Romeo and Juliet' by Shakespeare is a tragedy about two young lovers from feuding families in Verona, Italy
'Charlotte's Web' by E.B. White tells the story of a pig named Wilbur and a spider named Charlotte, exploring themes of friendship and life cycles
'To Kill a Mockingbird' by Harper Lee explores racial injustice in the American South through the eyes of Scout Finch
'The Great Gatsby' by F. Scott Fitzgerald depicts the American Dream and its corruption during the Jazz Age of the 1920s
'Where the Wild Things Are' by Maurice Sendak is a picture book about a boy named Max who sails to an island of wild creatures
'The Diary of a Young Girl' by Anne Frank is a nonfiction diary of a Jewish girl hiding from the Nazis during World War II
'A Wrinkle in Time' by Madeleine L'Engle is a science fantasy novel about a girl who travels through space and time to rescue her father
Dr. Seuss (Theodor Geisel) wrote 'The Cat in the Hat' and 'Green Eggs and Ham,' using simple vocabulary and rhyme to encourage early reading
'The Odyssey' by Homer is an ancient Greek epic poem about Odysseus's ten-year journey home after the Trojan War

common_errors.wrong: Shakespeare wrote novels
common_errors.correct: Shakespeare wrote plays (dramas) and sonnets (poems). He did not write novels. The novel form became popular later.

common_errors.wrong: 'To Kill a Mockingbird' is a true story
common_errors.correct: 'To Kill a Mockingbird' is a novel (fiction). While inspired by Harper Lee's childhood in Alabama, the characters and events are fictional.

common_errors.wrong: Anne Frank's diary is fiction
common_errors.correct: 'The Diary of a Young Girl' is a real diary written by Anne Frank during her time in hiding. It is nonfiction.

facts.statement: A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, similar to a paragraph in prose
A haiku is a three-line Japanese poem with 5 syllables, 7 syllables, and 5 syllables, traditionally about nature
Free verse is poetry without a regular rhyme scheme or meter, allowing the poet freedom of expression
A sonnet is a 14-line poem, often in iambic pentameter; Shakespearean sonnets have three quatrains and a couplet
A limerick is a humorous five-line poem with an AABBA rhyme scheme
A couplet is two consecutive lines of poetry that rhyme: 'Roses are red, violets are blue'
Rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhyming words at the end of each line, labeled with letters (ABAB, ABBA, AABB)
Meter is the rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in poetry; iambic pentameter has five pairs of unstressed/stressed syllables per line
A ballad is a narrative poem that tells a story, often meant to be sung, with a regular rhyme and rhythm

common_errors.wrong: a haiku must be about nature
common_errors.correct: Traditional Japanese haiku focus on nature, but modern English-language haiku can be about any topic. The 5-7-5 syllable structure is the defining feature.

common_errors.wrong: all sonnets follow the same rhyme scheme
common_errors.correct: Shakespearean (English) sonnets use ABABCDCDEFEFGG. Petrarchan (Italian) sonnets use ABBAABBA for the octave plus varied sestet patterns.

common_errors.wrong: free verse means the poem has no structure at all
common_errors.correct: Free verse lacks regular rhyme or meter but still uses line breaks, imagery, rhythm, and other literary devices deliberately.

common_errors.wrong: stanza and paragraph mean the same thing
common_errors.correct: A stanza is a grouping of lines in poetry. A paragraph is a grouping of sentences in prose. While similar in purpose, they belong to different forms.
